entries.definition: an act intending or showing kindness and good will
entries.label: positive
entries.tone: The broadest praise here, naming the good will driving the act as much as the act, whether the kindness lands or is only meant.

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: Formal and elevated, praising a kind act at a slight remove where *kindness* simply names it.

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: Credit for regard paid to someone else — the kindness lies in the care taken, not in warmth as such.

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: The most openly tender of these, since the act is affection displayed rather than care measured out.

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: The kindness comes as something granted graciously, which leaves the receiver holding an obligation *consideration* never creates.

entries.definition: the act of excusing a mistake or offense
entries.label: positive
entries.tone: Warmer and more inward than *pardon* for the same excusing — a wrong let go rather than officially remitted.

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: The plain warm name for the deed itself, with none of the ceremony *benignity* puts around the same act.
examples: whether Mrs. Collins has yet expressed her sense of your kindness in coming to us

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: Praises the noticing behind the deed, where *consideration* praises the regard the deed shows.

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Heavy and clumsy, a mistake big enough to leave the maker embarrassed by it.

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Informal and dismissive - the embarrassment is over a job made a mess of, not the single wrong step of *blunder*.

entries.definition: a mistake that results from taking one thing to be another
entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Names the mechanism - one thing taken for another - which lets the mistake sound explicable rather than culpable.
examples: he changed his name in order to avoid confusion with the notorious outlaw

entries.definition: the mistake of misrepresenting the facts
entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Named by its result - the facts come out bent - which makes it sound graver than a simple miss like *slip*.

entries.definition: a wrong action attributable to bad judgment or ignorance or inattention
entries.label: negative
entries.tone: The flattest of these three - the action is simply recorded as wrong, with no reach toward blame.

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Weightier than *foolishness* - the mistake is named as an act of unwisdom, and the word sounds like a verdict on it.
examples: Selling the land so cheaply was a folly he regretted for years.

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: The mildest of the stupid-mistake words, chiding where *stupidity* condemns.

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: The harshest here - a mistake treated as proof of an almost total want of mind.

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Attention gave way for a moment - blameable, but only lightly, and without the clumsiness of *blunder*.

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: The mistake lies in what went undone, and the neglect in it presses harder than the bare inattention of *oversight*.

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Something went unnoticed, and the word half-excuses the mistake in the act of naming it.

entries.definition: a minor inadvertent mistake usually observed in speech or writing or in small accidents or memory lapses etc.
entries.label: negative
entries.tone: The smallest and most forgivable, an unmeant slight miss in speech or writing, a small mishap, a memory that skipped.

entries.definition: an act that brings discredit to the person who does it
entries.label: negative
entries.tone: The discrediting act figured as a small mark - smaller, and easier to rub out, than *stain*.

entries.definition: an act that brings discredit to the person who does it
entries.label: negative
entries.tone: The discredit sticks - where *spot* can be wiped off, this one is taken to mark the doer.

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Blunt: the mistake is named by the mental failing behind it, so the contempt lands on the doer rather than the act.

entries.definition: have the skills and qualifications to do things well
entries.label: positive
entries.tone: The same compliment pitched cooler than *able* — an appraisal of what someone is equipped to do well rather than a warm word for them.
examples: children as young as 14 can be extremely capable and dependable
She proved a capable nurse through the long illness.

entries.definition: properly or sufficiently qualified or capable or efficient
entries.label: positive
entries.tone: The mildest approval here, since 'properly or sufficiently' sets a threshold and reports it met — qualified, capable or efficient enough, and no claim beyond enough.

entries.definition: able to accomplish a purpose; functioning effectively
entries.label: positive
entries.tone: Approval aimed at the working rather than the worker: the purpose is accomplished and the thing functions, which is a narrower compliment than *able*.
examples: the efficient cause of the revolution

entries.label: positive
entries.tone: Praises by holding the thing up to a standard-bearer — worthy of a good workman — which makes it concrete where *competent* stays abstract.
examples: the book is a workmanlike job with chronology and bibliography and index

entries.label: negative
entries.tone: Plain and unbuttoned beside the grander *lunacy*, making the same accusation of madness without the formality.
